weeks.title: Marketing Foundations
weeks.context:
Most people think marketing is posting on Instagram and running ads. That is the visible 10%. The invisible 90%, the part that decides whether the posts and ads work at all, is strategy: knowing exactly who you are selling to, what they want, why they should pick you over the next seller, and the path they take from never having heard of you to handing over their money. Skip this and you spend twelve weeks shouting into the void.

You are the new growth marketer for Adwoa Owusu, founder of Adwoa's Kitchen, an Accra food business. Adwoa cooks the best jollof in her neighbourhood and sells grilled food, plus she bottles her own jollof spice mix and pepper sauces to ship across Ghana. She is brilliant in the kitchen and invisible online: no followers, almost no website traffic, no steady stream of orders. Your mission across this track is to take Adwoa's Kitchen from zero to 10,000 followers and leads in twelve weeks.

This week you build the strategic foundation everything else stands on. By Sunday you will have a positioning statement (one sentence that says who Adwoa's Kitchen is for and why it wins) and a customer journey map (the step-by-step path a stranger walks to become a paying, repeat customer). These two documents are case study #1 in your portfolio, and the brief you will execute against for the next eleven weeks.

concept_check.q: Adwoa says 'my food is for everyone who likes good food.' Why is that a weak target market?
choices: It is too expensive to reach everyone
'Everyone' is not a market, you cannot write a message that moves a person you have not pictured
Good food is not a real selling point
It should be 'everyone in Accra' instead
concept_check.explain: When you target everyone you speak to no one. A specific person (a busy Accra office worker who misses home-cooked lunch) lets you write a message that actually lands. Niche down to scale up.

concept_check.q: A customer sees Adwoa's jollof on Instagram, visits the website, but does not buy. Where did the journey break?
choices: The product is bad
Somewhere between awareness and purchase, often the website did not make it easy or trustworthy to act
Instagram is the wrong channel
She should have run ads instead
concept_check.explain: Interest without action means a gap in the journey, usually a missing trust signal, an unclear next step, or friction at checkout. Mapping the journey is how you find and fix that gap.

concept_check.q: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit for Adwoa's spice mix?
choices: There is no difference
Feature = '12 hand-ground spices'; benefit = 'restaurant-taste jollof in 20 minutes, no measuring'
Benefit is the price, feature is the size
Features sell better than benefits
concept_check.explain: A feature is what it IS; a benefit is what it DOES for the customer's life. People buy benefits. 'Restaurant jollof in 20 minutes' sells; 'twelve spices' is just trivia until you connect it to the outcome.

topics: What marketing actually is (and is not)
Target market and the ideal customer (persona)
Positioning and differentiation
Features vs benefits, and the value proposition
The marketing funnel and the customer journey
The four Ps as a sanity check
Setting a goal and the one metric that matters

weeks.project: Produce the strategic brief for Adwoa's Kitchen: a one-page document containing (1) an ideal customer persona, (2) a positioning statement, (3) a value proposition with three benefit-led selling points, and (4) a customer journey map across awareness, consideration, purchase, and loyalty, noting the channel and the goal for each stage. This brief is the plan you execute for the rest of the track. Portfolio case study #1.
exercises: Interview-style notes: describe one real person who is the perfect Adwoa's Kitchen customer
Write three versions of the positioning statement and pick the sharpest
Convert a feature list into a benefit list
Draw the journey map and mark where the current biggest drop-off is
questions: Who exactly is Adwoa's Kitchen for, and who is it not for?
Why would someone choose Adwoa over the next jollof seller?
What is the path from never-heard-of-us to repeat customer?
outputs: A customer journey map with stages, channels, and goals
mastery_questions: State Adwoa's Kitchen target customer in one specific sentence
Write a positioning statement using the for / who / is / that / unlike formula
Turn any feature into a benefit
Name the four journey stages and one goal for each
Name the single metric you will judge the next 12 weeks by
weeks.ai_assist: Use an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) as a brainstorming partner, never as the final author. Good prompts this week: 'Act as a marketing strategist. Here is my business [paste details]. Help me draft 3 ideal-customer personas, then critique them for being too vague.' Always pressure-test the output against reality, you know the Ghanaian market and the AI does not.
pre_flight: A free Google account (for Google Docs)
A notebook or doc to capture ideas
Curiosity about real businesses around you
common_mistakes: Targeting 'everyone', which means targeting no one
Listing features (12 spices) instead of benefits (restaurant jollof in 20 minutes)
Copying a competitor's positioning instead of finding a real point of difference
Treating the journey as a single step (see ad, buy) instead of a path with stages
debug_help: Stuck on the persona? Picture ONE real person you know who would love this, and describe them.
Positioning feels generic? Add the 'unlike [alternative]' clause, it forces a real difference.
Journey map feels empty? Walk it yourself: how would YOU find, judge, and buy from a new food brand?

Find three real competitors and write one sentence on how each positions itself
resources: Your own observation of food businesses in your city

days.title: What marketing really is, and set up your workspace
days.summary: Today you'll learn what marketing actually is beneath the noise, then set up the free workspace and portfolio folder you will use for all twelve weeks.

items.title: Marketing is not posting, it is matching
items.body:
## The one-line definition
Marketing is **getting the right message, to the right person, at the right time, so they take an action**. That is it. Posting, ads, emails, SEO, those are just *channels*, the pipes the message travels through. Beginners obsess over the pipes (which app, which post). Professionals obsess over the *match*: who is this for, what do they need to hear, and what do we want them to do.

## Why strategy comes before tactics
Imagine Adwoa spends GHS 500 on Instagram ads for her spice mix. If she does not know *who* it is for, the ad says 'buy my spice mix' to random people, and almost nobody buys. Same GHS 500, but aimed at *busy Accra office workers who miss home-cooked food and cannot cook jollof properly*, with the message *'restaurant jollof in 20 minutes, no measuring'*, and now it converts. The money did not change. The **strategy** did. This week is that strategy.

## The three questions every marketer answers first
Before a single post goes out, you must be able to answer:

1. **Who exactly are we selling to?** (Not 'everyone'. A specific person.)
2. **Why should they pick us over the alternatives?** (Our positioning.)
3. **What path do we walk them down, from stranger to repeat buyer?** (The journey.)

If you cannot answer these, no amount of pretty posts will save the business. If you *can*, even average posts perform, because they are aimed.

## What you are building this week
By Sunday: a **positioning statement** (one sharp sentence) and a **customer journey map** (the path). Together they are the brief you will execute for eleven more weeks. Every later skill, content, social, SEO, ads, email, is just *delivering this strategy through a channel*. Get the strategy right and the rest is execution.

items.title: Set up your marketing workspace and portfolio
items.body:
## Do this now, before any lessons
You will produce twelve case studies over this track. Set up where they live, once, today.

**1. A Google account + Google Drive.** If you do not have one, create a free Gmail account (use `firstname.lastname@gmail.com` if you can, this is the address you will put on your marketing CV). Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, and Slides are all free and are what most marketing teams actually use.

**2. Your portfolio folder.** In Google Drive, create a folder named `Adwoa's Kitchen - Marketing Portfolio`. Inside it, create twelve sub-folders: `Week 01 Strategy` through `Week 12 Career`. Every week's deliverable goes in its folder. By Week 12 this folder *is* your portfolio.

**3. Your strategy doc.** In the Week 01 folder, create a Google Doc titled `Adwoa's Kitchen - Strategic Brief`. Paste in four headings now, each on its own line: `Ideal Customer`, `Positioning Statement`, `Value Proposition`, `Customer Journey Map`. You will fill these across the week.

**4. A swipe file.** Create one more doc: `Swipe File - good marketing I see`. Whenever you spot an ad, caption, or email that grabs you, screenshot it here with one line on *why* it worked. Top marketers all keep a swipe file. Start yours today.

Everything here is free. No paid tools this week, or for most of this track.

cards.prompt: Marketing is mainly about choosing the right app to post on.
cards.whenRight: Correct. The app is just a pipe. Marketing is the MATCH: right message, right person, right time. Strategy beats tool choice every time.
cards.whenWrong: Not quite. The channel (app) is just delivery. Marketing is matching the right message to the right person, the strategy under the posts.

cards.prompt: A specific target customer ('busy Accra office worker who misses home food') beats a broad one ('everyone who likes food').
cards.whenRight: Yes. A specific person lets you write a message that actually lands. 'Everyone' forces vague messaging that moves no one.
cards.whenWrong: Look again. Specific wins. You can only write a message that moves someone if you can picture exactly who they are.

cards.prompt: If an ad fails, the first thing to blame is the budget being too small.
cards.whenRight: Right. Usually it is the STRATEGY, wrong person or wrong message, not the budget. The same money aimed correctly converts.
cards.whenWrong: Usually not the budget. A failing ad most often has the wrong audience or message. Fix the aim before adding money.

items.title: Your turn, build your workspace
items.body:
Set up your foundation. Tick each only when it is actually done.

- [ ] Google account created or confirmed, with a clean address
- [ ] `Adwoa's Kitchen - Marketing Portfolio` folder created in Drive
- [ ] Twelve weekly sub-folders created (Week 01 to Week 12)
- [ ] `Strategic Brief` doc created with the four headings
- [ ] `Swipe File` doc created, with at least ONE example added today

Then write two sentences at the top of your Strategic Brief: *What does Adwoa's Kitchen sell, and what is the 12-week goal (zero to 10,000 followers and leads)?* You now have a home for everything that follows.

days.title: Orient, what you are building this week
days.summary: Today you'll see the full picture of the strategic brief you are producing this week, and why these two documents decide the success of the next eleven.

items.title: The brief that drives everything
items.body:
## Why this week matters more than any other
Every later week, content, social, SEO, ads, email, analytics, executes a *decision you make this week*. Choose the wrong customer and you will write content nobody wants, target ads at the wrong people, and optimise a website for the wrong buyer. The strategic brief is the steering wheel. Bad strategy executed brilliantly still drives off a cliff.

## The four pieces of the brief
1. **Ideal customer persona** (Day 2): one specific person who is the perfect buyer, their situation, problem, and what they care about.
2. **Positioning statement** (Day 3): one sentence, for whom, what we are, and why we win.
3. **Value proposition** (Day 4): three benefit-led reasons to buy, the actual words you will use in posts and ads.
4. **Customer journey map** (Day 5): the path from stranger to repeat buyer, stage by stage, with the channel and goal for each.

## A goal needs a number
'Grow Adwoa's Kitchen' is a wish, not a goal. A goal has a number and a deadline: *reach 10,000 combined followers and leads in twelve weeks.* And you need **one primary metric** to judge progress, here, total *leads* (people who give us their contact, follow, or order), because followers without leads do not pay the bills. Everything you build gets judged against that number.

## The mindset shift
Stop thinking 'what should I post?' Start thinking 'what does my specific customer need to see, at this stage of their journey, to take the next step?' That single reframe is the difference between a hobbyist who posts and a marketer who grows a business. This week you build the map; the rest of the track you follow it.

cards.prompt: 'Grow Adwoa's Kitchen' is a proper marketing goal.
cards.whenRight: Right. It has no number and no deadline. A real goal: 'reach 10,000 followers and leads in 12 weeks.' Numbers make progress measurable.
cards.whenWrong: It is a wish, not a goal. Add a NUMBER and a DEADLINE: '10,000 followers and leads in 12 weeks.' Then you can measure it.

cards.prompt: Followers matter more than leads for a business that needs to make money.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Followers are nice; LEADS (contacts, orders) pay the bills. The primary metric should track value, not vanity.
cards.whenWrong: Flip it. Followers can be a vanity metric. Leads, people who give contact or buy, are what fund the business.

cards.prompt: The strategic brief is the plan every later week executes against.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Content, social, SEO, ads, email, all deliver the strategy you set this week. The brief is the steering wheel.
cards.whenWrong: It is. Every later channel just executes this week's strategy. Get the brief right and the rest is delivery.

items.title: Your turn, commit to the goal
items.body:
In your Strategic Brief doc, write the goal and primary metric clearly at the top:

- [ ] **Goal:** a specific 12-week target (e.g. '10,000 combined followers + leads across channels')
- [ ] **Primary metric:** the ONE number you will judge progress by (recommend: total leads)
- [ ] **Why this metric:** one sentence on why it matters more than vanity numbers

Then list the four pieces of the brief you will complete this week, so future-you knows the plan. You have now framed the whole week.

days.title: Know your customer, the ideal persona
days.summary: Today you'll build a specific, vivid picture of the one person Adwoa's Kitchen is perfect for, the foundation of every message you will ever write.

items.title: Niche down to scale up
items.body:
## Why one person beats everyone
The biggest beginner mistake is 'my product is for everyone.' It feels safe, more people, more sales, right? Wrong. When you write for everyone, you write generic messages that move no one. When you write for *one specific person*, your message becomes sharp, and, surprisingly, it attracts *more* people, because it actually resonates with someone. This is the niche-to-scale paradox: get specific to grow big.

## What an ideal customer persona is
A persona is a detailed, semi-fictional portrait of your perfect customer, built from real observation. Not a demographic ('women 25-40'), a *person*. Give them a name, a life, a problem. For Adwoa's Kitchen, one strong persona:

> **Akosua, 29, Accra.** Works a busy 9-to-5 in a bank in Osu. Misses her mum's cooking but gets home at 8pm exhausted. Cannot cook jollof that tastes 'right'. Has money but no time. Scrolls Instagram on her commute. Cares about taste, convenience, and food that feels like home. Would happily pay for a spice mix that makes restaurant jollof in 20 minutes, or order a fresh grilled meal for the weekend.

Now you can *picture* her. You know what to say, what photo to show, what time to post (her commute), and what she will pay for.

## The persona questions
Build yours by answering: Who are they (name, age, location, work)? What is their *day* like? What problem do they have that you solve? What do they care about when buying food? Where do they spend time online? What would make them hesitate (price? trust? delivery?)? The more vivid, the more useful.

## One product can have a few personas
Adwoa's Kitchen might serve Akosua (busy office worker, buys spice mix + weekend meals) AND a corporate catering buyer (orders for office events). Different people, different messages. Start with the ONE who is most common and most profitable, that is your primary persona, the hero of your strategy.

Today you make Akosua (or your version) real on paper. Every future post, ad, and email is written *to her*.

cards.prompt: 'Women aged 25 to 40' is a strong customer persona.
cards.whenRight: Right, that is a demographic, not a person. A persona has a name, a life, a problem you can picture and write to.
cards.whenWrong: Too broad. That is a demographic. A persona is a specific person, Akosua, 29, busy banker, misses home food, with a life you can picture.

cards.prompt: Knowing your persona scrolls Instagram on her commute tells you WHEN to post.
cards.whenRight: Exactly. A vivid persona reveals timing, message, photo style, and price tolerance, all the practical decisions.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Her commute is your posting window. A rich persona answers the practical questions for you.

cards.prompt: Targeting one specific persona will shrink your total audience and hurt growth.
cards.whenRight: Correct, the opposite. Specific messages resonate and attract MORE people. Niche down to scale up.
cards.whenWrong: It is the reverse. Specific, resonant messaging attracts more people than vague 'for everyone' messaging. Niche to scale.

items.title: Your turn, build the persona
items.body:
In your Strategic Brief under `Ideal Customer`, write a full persona for Adwoa's Kitchen:

- [ ] Name, age, location, job
- [ ] A paragraph on their typical day
- [ ] The specific problem Adwoa's Kitchen solves for them
- [ ] What they care about most when buying food (taste? time? trust? price?)
- [ ] Where they spend time online, and when
- [ ] Their #1 hesitation before buying

Make it vivid enough that a stranger could read it and picture a real person. Tip: base it loosely on someone you actually know. This persona is the reader of everything you write from now on.

days.title: Positioning, why you and not them
days.summary: Today you'll write the single most important sentence in marketing: the positioning statement that says who you are for and why you win.

items.title: The one sentence that decides everything
items.body:
## What positioning is
Positioning is the place your brand occupies in the customer's mind, the answer to *'why should I pick you over the alternatives?'* Akosua has options: cook herself, buy from a chop bar, order from a competitor, use a different spice. Positioning is the reason she picks Adwoa's Kitchen. Without it, you are just 'another jollof seller', competing on price (a race to the bottom).

## The positioning formula
A classic, reliable template:

> **For** [target customer] **who** [need or situation], **[brand]** **is** [category] **that** [key benefit / point of difference], **unlike** [main alternative].

Filled in for Adwoa's Kitchen:

> *For busy Accra professionals who miss real home-cooked food but have no time to cook, Adwoa's Kitchen is a homemade-food brand that delivers restaurant-quality jollof and grills (and a spice mix that does it in 20 minutes), unlike fast food that fills you up but never tastes like home.*

Read it again. It names *who* (busy pros), the *need* (home food, no time), the *category* (homemade food), the *difference* (restaurant-quality, fast), and the *alternative it beats* (soulless fast food). That one sentence now guides every photo, caption, and ad.

## The 'unlike' clause is the magic
Most brands skip the 'unlike' and end up generic ('we sell great food'). The *unlike* forces you to name a real point of difference against a real alternative. If you cannot finish the 'unlike' clause, you have not found your edge yet, keep digging. Adwoa's edge might be *taste of home*, *speed*, *consistency*, or *the spice mix nobody else sells*. Pick the one that is true and that Akosua cares about most.

## Positioning is a choice, and a sacrifice
Strong positioning means *not* being for everyone. By positioning as 'home-cooked food for busy professionals', you give up the 'cheapest street food' crowd, on purpose. That focus is what makes the message powerful. Trying to be everything to everyone is how brands become invisible.

Today you write three versions and pick the sharpest. This sentence is the spine of your whole strategy.

cards.prompt: Good positioning tries to appeal to as many different customers as possible.
cards.whenRight: Right. Strong positioning means choosing who you are NOT for. Focus is what makes the message land. Be everything to everyone and you are invisible.
cards.whenWrong: The opposite. Positioning is a choice and a sacrifice, you focus on a specific customer and edge, and deliberately give up the rest.

cards.prompt: The 'unlike [alternative]' clause forces you to name a real point of difference.
cards.whenRight: Yes. If you cannot finish 'unlike...', you have not found your edge. That clause is what stops positioning from being generic.
cards.whenWrong: It does. The 'unlike' clause is the magic, it forces a real, specific difference against a real alternative.

cards.prompt: Without positioning, a food brand usually ends up competing mainly on price.
cards.whenRight: Correct. No clear reason to pick you = a race to the bottom on price. Positioning gives a reason beyond 'cheapest'.
cards.whenWrong: It is true. With no point of difference, the only lever left is price, a race to the bottom. Positioning escapes that.

items.title: Your turn, write the positioning
items.body:
In your Strategic Brief under `Positioning Statement`:

- [ ] Write THREE versions using the formula: For [who] who [need], [brand] is [category] that [difference], unlike [alternative]
- [ ] For each, make sure the 'unlike' names a real alternative and a real edge
- [ ] Read all three aloud, pick the sharpest, and mark it as the final
- [ ] Write one sentence on what you are deliberately NOT (who Adwoa's Kitchen is not for)

The final statement should make Akosua nod and think 'that is exactly what I need.' If it could describe any food seller, it is not sharp enough yet.

days.title: Features vs benefits, the value proposition
days.summary: Today you'll learn the single most important copywriting skill, turning what a product IS into what it DOES for the customer, and build Adwoa's value proposition.

items.title: Nobody buys features, they buy better lives
items.body:
## The most expensive mistake in marketing
Beginners describe their product: '12 hand-ground spices, 200g jar, locally sourced.' Those are **features**, facts about the product. Customers do not care about features. They care about what the features *do for them*. Akosua does not want '12 spices'; she wants *restaurant-taste jollof in 20 minutes without measuring anything*. That is a **benefit**, the outcome in her life. People buy benefits. Always.

## Feature to benefit, the 'so what?' test
Take any feature and ask 'so what?' until you reach the human outcome:

- '12 hand-ground spices' → so what? → 'perfectly balanced flavour' → so what? → **'jollof that tastes like a top restaurant made it, every time'**
- 'pre-measured mix' → so what? → 'no guessing, no measuring' → so what? → **'cook confidently even if you have never made good jollof'**
- 'ships across Ghana, frozen' → so what? → 'arrives fresh anywhere' → so what? → **'taste of home delivered to your door, wherever you are'**

The bolded endpoints are what you put in captions and ads. The features become *supporting proof*, not the headline.

## The value proposition
Your **value proposition** is the short, benefit-led answer to 'why should I buy this?', usually a headline plus two or three benefit points. For Adwoa's spice mix:

> **Restaurant jollof in 20 minutes.**
> - Tastes like a top Accra restaurant, every single time (no skill needed)
> - Pre-measured, no guessing, just add rice and follow three steps
> - Made in Accra from real spices, the taste of home in a jar

Notice the features (real spices, pre-measured) appear, but *attached to a benefit*. That is the formula: benefit first, feature as proof.

## Why this skill pays for itself
Every caption, ad, email subject line, and product page lives or dies on benefit-led copy. The same product, described as features, gets ignored; described as benefits, sells. You will use this 'so what?' test every single week of this track. Master it now.

Today you turn Adwoa's product features into benefits and assemble her value proposition.

cards.prompt: '200g jar, 12 spices, locally sourced' is benefit-led copy that will sell well.
cards.whenRight: Right, those are features. They sell only once you connect them to a benefit: 'restaurant jollof in 20 minutes, no skill needed.'
cards.whenWrong: Those are features (facts about the product). They sell when turned into benefits, what they DO for the customer's life.

cards.prompt: The 'so what?' test turns a feature into the human outcome a customer actually wants.
cards.whenRight: Exactly. Keep asking 'so what?' until you reach the benefit in their life. That endpoint is your headline.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Ask 'so what?' of any feature, repeatedly, until you reach the real-life outcome. That is the benefit.

cards.prompt: In good copy, features should still appear, but attached to a benefit as proof.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Benefit first ('cook confidently'), feature as proof ('pre-measured'). Features support, benefits sell.
cards.whenWrong: Correct, they should. Lead with the benefit, then use the feature as supporting proof. Not features alone.

items.title: Your turn, build the value proposition
items.body:
In your Strategic Brief under `Value Proposition`:

- [ ] List 4-5 real features of Adwoa's products (spice mix and/or meals)
- [ ] Run each through the 'so what?' test until you reach a human benefit
- [ ] Write a one-line value-proposition headline (benefit-led, like 'Restaurant jollof in 20 minutes')
- [ ] Write three benefit points underneath, each with the feature attached as proof

Read it as Akosua would. Does it make her want it? If it reads like a product spec sheet, you are still in feature-land, push each line through 'so what?' again.

days.title: The customer journey, stranger to superfan
days.summary: Today you'll map the full path a customer walks from never hearing of Adwoa's Kitchen to becoming a loyal repeat buyer, the master plan for the whole track.

items.title: Nobody buys on the first touch
items.body:
## The journey, not the leap
Marketing beginners imagine a single moment: person sees ad, person buys. Reality is a *journey* of many touches. Akosua might see a reel, follow the account, read a few posts over a week, click to the website, read reviews, leave, come back, then finally order. Your job is to understand and smooth every step of that path. This is the **customer journey** (or marketing funnel), and mapping it is how you find exactly where people drop off.

## The four stages
1. **Awareness** (top of funnel): they discover you exist. Goal: get seen by the right people. Channels: social reels, SEO, word of mouth, ads. Here you do not sell, you attract and earn attention.
2. **Consideration** (middle): they are interested and judging you. Goal: build trust and desire. Channels: helpful content, reviews, behind-the-scenes, email. Here you prove you are worth it.
3. **Purchase** (bottom): they are ready to buy. Goal: make buying easy and safe. Channels: website, WhatsApp order, a clear offer, a smooth checkout. Here you remove friction.
4. **Loyalty** (post-purchase): they bought, now keep them. Goal: turn buyers into repeat customers and advocates. Channels: email, follow-up, loyalty perks, asking for reviews. The cheapest sale is to someone who already trusts you.

## A different message for each stage
The mistake is using the same 'BUY NOW' message everywhere. You would not propose marriage on a first date. At *awareness*, a hard sell scares people off, give value (a recipe tip, a mouth-watering reel). At *purchase*, being shy and not asking for the order loses the sale. Match the message to the stage. The journey map tells you which message goes where.

## Find the leak
Most businesses have one stage that leaks badly. Adwoa might get *lots* of awareness (people see her food) but lose them at consideration (no website, no reviews, no easy way to order, no trust). Mapping the journey makes the leak obvious, and that leak is exactly where the next eleven weeks of work should focus. For Adwoa, weeks 2-3 fix awareness and consideration (content + social), weeks 4-7 widen awareness (SEO + ads), week 8 builds loyalty (email).

Today you draw the full map and mark the biggest current leak. This map is your campaign plan.

cards.prompt: Most customers buy the first time they see a brand.
cards.whenRight: Right. Buying is a journey of many touches, discover, follow, consider, trust, then buy. Plan for the path, not a single leap.
cards.whenWrong: Rarely. People take many touches to buy. Your job is to map and smooth the whole journey, not expect a one-touch sale.

cards.prompt: You should use a hard 'BUY NOW' message at every stage of the journey.
cards.whenRight: Correct. Match message to stage. At awareness, give value, do not hard-sell. Save the strong ask for the purchase stage.
cards.whenWrong: No, match the message to the stage. A hard sell at awareness scares people off. Give value early, ask for the order later.

cards.prompt: Mapping the journey helps you find the single stage where you are losing the most people.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Every business has a leaky stage. The map exposes it, and that leak is where your effort should focus.
cards.whenWrong: It does. The map reveals your biggest leak, the stage losing the most people, so you know where to focus.

items.title: Your turn, map the journey
items.body:
In your Strategic Brief under `Customer Journey Map`, build the map for Adwoa's Kitchen:

- [ ] For each of the four stages (Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, Loyalty): write the customer's mindset, the goal, the channel(s), and the kind of message that fits
- [ ] Mark where you believe the biggest current LEAK is (where Adwoa loses the most people)
- [ ] Write one sentence connecting that leak to the upcoming weeks that will fix it

You now have the master plan: a persona, a position, a value prop, and the path. Tomorrow you assemble and polish it into the finished brief.

days.title: Assemble and pressure-test the strategy
days.summary: Today you'll combine the four pieces into one coherent strategic brief and stress-test it, making sure every part points at the same customer and goal.

items.title: A strategy is only as strong as its alignment
items.body:
## The coherence test
You have four pieces: persona, positioning, value proposition, journey. A strong strategy is not four good pieces, it is four pieces that *point the same direction*. The persona (Akosua), the positioning (home food for busy pros), the value prop (restaurant jollof in 20 minutes), and the journey (where Akosua is and what she needs) must all describe the *same customer* solving the *same problem*. If your persona is a busy professional but your value prop talks about 'cheapest food in town', they are fighting each other. Today you align them.

## Pressure-test with these questions
Walk your brief through each:

- **Is the persona one specific person, not 'everyone'?** If still vague, sharpen it.
- **Does the positioning name a real difference (the 'unlike')?** If it could describe any seller, dig deeper.
- **Is the value prop benefit-led, not a feature list?** Run any feature-y line through 'so what?' again.
- **Does the journey have a different goal and message per stage?** And is the biggest leak identified?
- **Do all four describe the SAME customer and problem?** This is the big one.

## The 'so what would you actually do?' check
A strategy must be *actionable*. For each journey stage, you should be able to name a concrete thing you will build in the coming weeks. Awareness → reels and SEO (weeks 2-7). Consideration → helpful content and reviews. Purchase → a clean website and easy ordering. Loyalty → email follow-ups (week 8). If a stage has no plan, your map has a gap. The brief should read like a campaign you could hand to someone and they would know exactly what to do.

## Use AI to critique, not to create
Paste your brief into an AI assistant with the prompt: *'You are a sharp marketing strategist. Critique this brief for vagueness, misalignment, and any stage missing a plan. Be tough.'* The AI will not know the Ghanaian market like you do, so judge its feedback, but it is excellent at spotting where you have been lazy or generic. Fix what it correctly flags.

Today you produce the finished, aligned, pressure-tested brief, your first portfolio case study.

## From working doc to portfolio piece
Your brief is done; now make it *showable*. A portfolio piece is not just the work, it is the work *presented so a stranger (or employer, or client) instantly gets it*. The difference between 'I did strategy' and a clean, titled, well-formatted one-pager is the difference between getting hired and getting skipped. Spend the last hour on presentation.

## What case study #1 must contain
A single clean document (Google Doc, or a one-page Canva/Slides layout) titled **Adwoa's Kitchen, Marketing Strategy Brief**, with:

- A one-line **context**: what Adwoa's Kitchen is and the 12-week goal
- The **ideal customer persona** (the vivid one)
- The **positioning statement** (the final, sharp sentence)
- The **value proposition** (headline + three benefit points)
- The **customer journey map** (four stages, each with goal, channel, message; leak marked)
- A closing line: the primary metric you will judge success by

## Write the 'case study' framing
At the very top, add two sentences a future employer reads first: *'The challenge: Adwoa's Kitchen had a great product but no strategy, no clear customer, position, or plan. The approach: I built a full strategic brief, persona, positioning, value proposition, and a customer journey map, to guide a 12-week growth campaign.'* That framing turns a document into a *story of what you did*, which is what gets you hired.

## Commit it to your portfolio
Save the finished brief in your `Week 01 Strategy` folder. This is permanent, it is case study #1 of twelve, and it is the plan every later week executes. You have not 'learned strategy'; you have *produced a real strategic asset* for a real-shaped business. That is the portfolio-first mindset that will define this whole track.

Next week: content marketing. You will take this strategy and turn it into a month of content that attracts Akosua, the awareness and consideration stages of your journey, made real.

weeks.title: Content Marketing
weeks.context:
Last week you built the strategy. This week you start filling the journey's awareness and consideration stages with the thing that actually attracts and earns trust: content. Content marketing is creating genuinely useful or entertaining material (posts, videos, recipes, tips) that pulls your ideal customer toward you, instead of interrupting them with ads. Done right, it is the cheapest, most durable growth engine a small business has.

For Adwoa's Kitchen, content is a natural fit, food is visual, emotional, and shareable. But 'just post food photos' is not a strategy. This week you learn to plan content with purpose: the value-first principle, content pillars, the hook, and a repeatable calendar so Adwoa is never staring at a blank screen wondering what to post.

By Sunday you will have produced a one-month content calendar AND ten finished pieces of content (captions, a short script, simple Canva graphics), all aimed at Akosua and tied to your Week 1 strategy. That calendar plus the ten pieces is case study #2, and the raw material that feeds next week's social media plan.

items.title: Give before you ask
items.body:
## The shift from interrupting to attracting
Old marketing *interrupts*: an ad jumps in front of you uninvited. Content marketing *attracts*: you make something so useful or enjoyable that people choose to follow you. For a small business with little budget, this is the great equaliser, you cannot outspend big brands on ads, but you can out-*help* and out-*entertain* them with content.

## The 80/20 rule
The core principle: roughly **80% of your content should GIVE value** (a cooking tip, a behind-the-scenes story, a laugh, a recipe), and only about **20% should directly SELL**. Most beginners flip this, they sell in every post, and watch their reach and trust collapse. Think of it like a friendship: someone who only ever asks you for things is exhausting; someone who gives, helps, and entertains is someone you want to hear from. Be the second one. The selling, when it comes, then *works*, because you have earned the right to ask.

## Why this is perfect for Adwoa
Food is the easiest content there is: it is visual, emotional, and tied to memory and home. Akosua does not want to be sold to on her commute, but she *will* stop for a mouth-watering jollof reel, a '3 mistakes that ruin your stew' tip, or a story of why Adwoa started cooking. Each of those builds the trust that eventually turns into an order. Content is how you fill the awareness and consideration stages of your Week 1 journey.

## This week's destination
By Day 7: a month's content calendar and ten finished pieces. Not random posts, planned content tied to pillars and aimed at Akosua. You will never again stare at a blank screen wondering what to post.

## Get the tool ready now
**Canva** is a free, browser-based design tool that lets non-designers make professional graphics, social posts, and simple videos using templates. Nearly every small-business marketer uses it. Set it up today.

**1. Create a free account** at canva.com (Google sign-in is fine). The free tier is more than enough for this whole track.

**2. Set Adwoa's brand basics.** Pick TWO brand colours (e.g. a warm tomato-red and a deep green, jollof colours) and note their hex codes. Pick ONE clean font for headings. Consistency in colour and font is 80% of looking professional. Write these in a doc called `Adwoa's Kitchen, Brand Basics` (you will expand it in Week 11).

**3. Explore one template.** Search Canva for 'Instagram post', open any food template, and change the text and colours to Adwoa's. Notice how fast you can make something clean. That is the whole point, you are not designing from scratch, you are adapting templates.

**4. Make a content folder.** In Canva, create a folder 'Adwoa's Kitchen' to keep your designs in one place.

Free, fast, and the foundation of every graphic you will make. No design skills required, just good templates and consistent colours.

items.title: Pillars: the cure for 'what do I post?'
items.body:
## The blank-screen problem
The number one reason small businesses stop posting is not laziness, it is *not knowing what to post*. They post randomly for two weeks, run dry, and quit. **Content pillars** solve this permanently. A pillar is a recurring theme your content keeps returning to. Instead of inventing posts from nothing, you rotate through your pillars, each one an endless well of ideas.

## Adwoa's four pillars (an example)
1. **Recipes and tips** (value): 'the secret to non-mushy jollof', '3 stew mistakes'. Pure value, builds authority and saves.
2. **Behind-the-scenes** (trust/story): Adwoa cooking, the market run, packing orders. People buy from people, this builds connection.
3. **Customer love** (social proof): reviews, photos of happy customers, repeat-order stories. Proof that others trust her.
4. **Product and offers** (the 20% sell): the spice mix, weekly specials, how to order. The direct ask, earned by the other three.

Notice three of four pillars are value/trust, and one sells. That *is* the 80/20 rule, built into your plan.

## Why four (not ten, not one)
Too few pillars and the account feels repetitive. Too many and it loses identity. Three to five is the sweet spot. Each pillar should connect to your strategy: Akosua wants taste, convenience, and a sense of home, so recipes (taste), behind-the-scenes (home), and customer love (trust) all serve her directly.

## Pillars make a calendar trivial
Once you have pillars, planning a week is just: Monday recipe, Wednesday behind-the-scenes, Friday customer love, Sunday offer. Rotate. You will see how fast a calendar comes together once the pillars exist. Today you define Adwoa's.

cards.whenWrong: That is exactly it. Pillars are your recurring themes (recipes, behind-the-scenes, customer love, offers) that you rotate through.

cards.whenRight: Right. Too many pillars loses identity. Three to five is the sweet spot, focused but not repetitive.

days.title: The hook, winning the first 3 seconds
days.summary: Today you'll learn the most important content skill, the hook, and write ten scroll-stopping openers for Adwoa's content.

items.title: No hook, no views
items.body:
## The brutal truth about attention
On social media, you have about **1 to 3 seconds** to stop someone's scroll. If the opening, the **hook**, does not grab them, nothing else matters. The most valuable recipe, the best photo, the deepest story, all wasted if the first line or first frame is boring. Professionals spend more time on the hook than on the rest of the content combined. So will you.

## What makes a hook work
Hooks work by creating a *reason to keep watching/reading*. The main types:

- **Curiosity gap:** 'The mistake that ruins 90% of jollof.' You *have* to know what it is.
- **Bold claim:** 'This is the only jollof recipe you will ever need.'
- **Relatable problem:** 'Your jollof keeps coming out mushy? Here is why.'
- **Surprising fact:** 'Most restaurants do THIS one thing to their rice that you do not.'
- **How-to promise:** 'How to get smoky party-jollof flavour on a normal stove.'

Each gives the viewer a reason to stay. A flat opener ('Here is our menu', 'Good morning everyone') gives none, and gets skipped.

## Hook for the format
On a **reel/TikTok**, the hook is the first spoken line AND the first visual frame (show the finished jollof, then 'here is the mistake...'). On a **caption or carousel**, the hook is the first line (the rest is hidden until they tap 'more', so line one must earn the tap). On a **blog/email**, the hook is the headline and first sentence. Same principle everywhere: earn the next second.

## Write ten, keep three
Good hooks are written in volume, then filtered. Pros write 10-20 hook options and pick the strongest. Today you write ten hooks for Adwoa's pillars and rate each by one test: *does it make me need to know more?* If you would scroll past it, so will Akosua.

cards.prompt: You have roughly 1 to 3 seconds to stop a scroll before the content is skipped.
cards.whenRight: Yes. The hook (first line/frame) is everything. Spend more time on it than on the rest of the content.
cards.whenWrong: That is the reality. The first 1-3 seconds decide it. If the hook fails, the best content underneath is wasted.

cards.prompt: 'Good morning everyone, here is our menu today' is a strong hook.
cards.whenRight: Right, it is flat, no curiosity or reason to stay. 'The mistake that ruins your jollof' stops the scroll; a menu greeting does not.
cards.whenWrong: It is weak, no reason to keep watching. Use a curiosity gap, bold claim, or relatable problem instead.

cards.prompt: The best way to get a great hook is to write many options and pick the strongest.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Write 10-20, filter to the best. Volume then selection beats trying to nail it in one try.
cards.whenWrong: It is. Pros write lots of hook options and choose the sharpest. Quantity then quality.

days.title: Captions, CTAs, and the full piece
days.summary: Today you'll turn hooks into complete content pieces with captions that hold attention and calls to action that tell people what to do next.

items.title: From hook to action
items.body:
## The anatomy of a content piece
A hook earns the first second; now you need the rest. A complete social piece has three parts: **Hook** (stop the scroll), **Body** (deliver the value or story, keep it tight), and **CTA** (call to action, tell them the one thing to do next). Most beginners nail none of these; you will nail all three.

## Writing the body
After the hook, deliver fast. People do not read, they skim. Keep sentences short. Use line breaks (white space) so a caption is scannable, not a wall of text. Deliver the promise the hook made: if your hook was 'the mistake that ruins jollof', the body reveals the mistake clearly and gives the fix. Do not pad. Every line should earn the next.

## The CTA: one clear next step
Here is where most engaged viewers are lost: the content is great, then... nothing. No instruction. The viewer enjoyed it and scrolls on. A **call to action** tells them the single next step: *'Save this for your next cook.'* *'Comment JOLLOF and I will send you the recipe.'* *'Tap the link to order the spice mix.'* *'Follow for a tip every week.'* One CTA per piece, never five. Match it to the journey stage: value posts → 'save/follow/comment' (build the relationship); selling posts → 'order/click the link' (the ask).

## Repurpose: one idea, many pieces
The pro secret to never running dry: one idea becomes many pieces. 'The 3 mistakes that ruin jollof' can be a *reel* (video), a *carousel* (3 slides), a *story poll* ('which mistake are you guilty of?'), and a *blog post* (for SEO, Week 4). One hour of thinking, four pieces of content. You will use this constantly to fill a calendar without burning out.

Today you assemble several complete pieces, hook plus body plus CTA, ready to post.

cards.whenRight: Right, ONE clear CTA. Multiple asks confuse people and reduce action. Tell them the single next step.
cards.whenWrong: Use ONE CTA. Multiple asks split attention and lower the chance anyone acts. One clear next step wins.

cards.prompt: Captions should be dense paragraphs to show you have lots to say.
cards.whenRight: Right, people skim. Short sentences and line breaks (white space) make captions scannable and far more likely to be read.
cards.whenWrong: The opposite, dense text gets skipped. Short lines and white space make a caption readable.

cards.whenRight: Yes. Repurposing one idea into many formats is how you fill a calendar without running out of ideas.
cards.whenWrong: It can. One idea = many pieces across formats. That is the secret to a full calendar without burnout.

days.title: Make it look good, simple Canva graphics
days.summary: Today you'll design clean, on-brand graphics in Canva for your content, learning the few rules that make amateur designs look professional.

items.title: Design rules even non-designers can follow
items.body:
## You do not need to be a designer
Good marketing design is not artistic talent, it is following a few rules consistently. With Canva templates and these rules, your graphics will look professional without any design training.

## The five rules
1. **Consistency beats creativity.** Use your two brand colours and one font on *everything*. A consistent look makes a brand feel established and trustworthy. Changing fonts and colours every post looks amateur.
2. **One message per graphic.** Do not cram. A graphic should communicate one idea in a glance. If you need more, use a carousel (multiple slides), not a crowded single image.
3. **Contrast for readability.** Text must be readable at a glance and on a small phone. Dark text on light background or light text on a dark overlay. If you cannot read it instantly, neither can Akosua.
4. **Use real photos.** For food, real photos of Adwoa's actual food beat any stock image. Good light (near a window), clean background, shot from above or at an angle. Your phone is enough.
5. **White space is your friend.** Do not fill every pixel. Empty space makes a design feel premium and the message pop.

## The template workflow
Never start from blank. Search Canva for the format ('Instagram post', 'reel cover', 'carousel'), pick a clean template close to your style, then swap in Adwoa's colours, font, photo, and text. Five minutes per graphic once you have the rhythm. Save a couple as *your* templates so future posts are even faster.

## Match the graphic to the format
A reel needs a strong *cover frame* (the thumbnail that makes people tap). A carousel needs slides that flow (slide 1 = hook, last slide = CTA). A quote/tip post needs big readable text. Today you make graphics for several of your pieces, applying the five rules.

cards.prompt: Changing fonts and colours on every post keeps the brand fresh and exciting.
cards.whenRight: Right, consistency wins. Same colours and font on everything makes a brand look established and trustworthy. Constant change looks amateur.
cards.whenWrong: Consistency beats novelty here. Keep the same brand colours and font, that is what looks professional.

cards.prompt: For a food brand, real photos of the actual food usually beat stock images.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Authentic photos of Adwoa's real food build trust and appetite. Stock food images feel generic and fake.
cards.whenWrong: Real beats stock for food. Authentic photos of the actual product are more appetising and trustworthy.

cards.whenRight: Yes. One message per graphic. If you have more, use a carousel rather than cramming one crowded image.
cards.whenWrong: It should. One idea per graphic; use a carousel for more. Crowded designs fail to land any message.

days.title: The content calendar, planning a month
days.summary: Today you'll build a one-month content calendar that turns your pillars and pieces into a clear, repeatable posting schedule.

items.title: A calendar turns chaos into a system
items.body:
## Why a calendar changes everything
Without a calendar, content is reactive: you scramble each day, post inconsistently, and burn out. With a calendar, content is a *system*: you plan a month in one sitting, batch-create, and post consistently without stress. Consistency, not perfection, is what grows an audience, and a calendar is what makes consistency possible.

## What goes in a content calendar
A simple calendar (a Google Sheet is perfect) has a row per planned post with columns: **Date**, **Pillar**, **Format** (reel/carousel/story/post), **Hook/Topic**, **Caption** (or link to it), **CTA**, **Status** (idea / drafted / designed / scheduled / posted). At a glance you see the month, balanced across pillars and formats, with nothing falling through.

## Balance the calendar
A good month is *balanced*. Check: Are most posts value (not selling)? The 80/20 rule should be visible, mostly value pillars, a few offers. Is there a mix of formats (some reels, some carousels, some stories)? Reels drive reach (awareness), carousels and tips drive saves and trust (consideration), offers drive sales (purchase). A calendar that is all selling, or all one format, is unbalanced. Spread across your Week 1 journey stages.

## Realistic cadence
For a small business, 3-5 posts a week is plenty and sustainable, do not promise daily and then quit by week two. Consistency at a pace you can keep beats a heroic burst followed by silence. Plan a month of about 12-16 posts. Batch the creation: write all captions in one session, design all graphics in another. Batching is far faster than doing one post a day from scratch.

Today you lay out a full month, pulling in the pieces you have already made.

cards.prompt: Posting daily and then quitting after two weeks beats posting 4 times a week consistently.
cards.whenRight: Right, consistency wins. A sustainable 3-5 posts/week for months beats a daily burst that collapses. Pick a pace you can keep.
cards.whenWrong: Consistency beats intensity. A steady 3-5/week sustained beats an unsustainable daily sprint that ends in silence.

cards.prompt: A content calendar should be balanced across pillars and formats, not all selling or all one format.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Balance keeps the 80/20 rule visible and serves every journey stage, reels for reach, tips for trust, offers for sales.
cards.whenWrong: It should be balanced. Mostly value, a few offers; a mix of formats. Imbalance (all selling, all reels) hurts results.

cards.prompt: Batching (writing all captions in one session, designing all graphics in another) is faster than daily one-offs.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Batching by task is far more efficient and is how a calendar gets built in one sitting.
cards.whenWrong: Batching wins. Doing all of one task at once beats context-switching to make one post per day.

items.title: Your turn, build the calendar
items.body:
Create a Google Sheet `Adwoa's Kitchen, Content Calendar`:

- [ ] Set up columns: Date, Pillar, Format, Hook/Topic, Caption, CTA, Status
- [ ] Plan a full month (12-16 posts) balanced across pillars and formats

You now have a month planned. Tomorrow you finish the ten pieces to a polished, post-ready standard.

days.title: Finish ten post-ready pieces
days.summary: Today you'll polish your content into ten complete, post-ready pieces, the tangible proof of your content skill.

items.title: Done and post-ready, not perfect
items.body:
## What 'post-ready' means
A post-ready piece needs nothing else before it goes live: it has a strong hook, a tight caption with white space, one clear CTA, the right hashtags/format, and (where relevant) a finished graphic or a clear video script. Today you take your drafts across that finish line. The goal is ten complete pieces, the raw fuel for next week's social plan.

## The polish checklist
For each piece, check: Does the hook stop the scroll? Is the caption skimmable (short lines, white space)? Is there exactly one CTA, matched to the journey stage? Is the value real (would Akosua genuinely find this useful or enjoyable)? Is it on-brand (colours, voice)? Are there a few relevant hashtags (e.g. #AccraFood #JollofRice #GhanaFoodie, you will go deeper on these in Week 3)? If yes to all, it is post-ready.

## Mix the ten across the journey
Your ten pieces should not all do the same job. Aim for roughly: 4-5 pure *value* pieces (recipes, tips, behind-the-scenes) for awareness and trust, 2-3 *social proof* pieces (customer love), and 2-3 *offer* pieces (the spice mix, how to order) for the purchase stage. That spread mirrors your journey map, you are not just making content, you are feeding every stage of the funnel.

## Write in Adwoa's voice
Content should sound like a warm, confident Accra cook, not a corporate brand and not raw AI text. Use natural language, a little local flavour, and Adwoa's personality. If you used AI to draft, *edit it* until it sounds human and specific (a real dish, a real customer, a real kitchen moment). Generic content gets ignored; authentic content gets shared. This voice is part of the brand you will define in Week 11.

Today you finish all ten. Tomorrow you package them and the calendar as case study #2.

cards.prompt: Your ten pieces should all do the same job to keep the message consistent.
cards.whenRight: Right, spread them across the journey: value, social proof, and offers. Each stage of the funnel needs feeding.
cards.whenWrong: Mix them. Some value, some social proof, some offers, so you feed awareness, consideration, AND purchase.

cards.prompt: Content should sound like Adwoa (a warm, real Accra cook), not generic AI or corporate text.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Authentic, human, specific content gets shared; generic content gets scrolled past. Edit any AI draft until it sounds real.
cards.whenWrong: Voice matters. Make it sound like a real person with local flavour, not generic AI or corporate copy.

cards.prompt: 'Post-ready' means a piece needs nothing else before it can go live.
cards.whenRight: Yes, hook, caption, one CTA, format/hashtags, and visual all done. That is the standard for your ten pieces.
cards.whenWrong: It does, fully finished and ready to publish as-is. That is the bar for each of your ten pieces.

Ten finished pieces plus a month's calendar, that is real, showable work. Tomorrow you ship it.

days.title: Ship it, content calendar + 10 pieces (case study #2)
days.summary: Today you'll package the content calendar and ten finished pieces into case study #2 of your portfolio.

items.title: Ship it, and frame the result
items.body:
## Package case study #2
You have a month's content calendar and ten finished pieces. Now present them as a portfolio case study. Create one document or Canva/Slides layout titled **Adwoa's Kitchen, Content Marketing System**, containing:

- A short **context + challenge** line: Adwoa had no content plan and posted randomly (or not at all)
- Your **content pillars** and why each was chosen
- The **one-month content calendar** (a screenshot of the sheet is fine)
- The **ten finished pieces** (graphics + captions), neatly laid out
- A one-line note on how this feeds the awareness and consideration stages of the Week 1 journey

## The case-study framing again
Open with the challenge/approach story: *'The challenge: a great food brand with no content engine, no plan, no consistency. The approach: I built a pillar-based content system, a one-month calendar, and ten ready-to-post pieces aimed at the target customer.'* This framing is what makes an employer see a *marketer who builds systems*, not just someone who can make a post.

## Why content is your durable engine
Ads stop the moment you stop paying. Content keeps working, a great reel or blog post can attract customers for months or years. By building Adwoa a content *system* (not just posts), you have given her a growth engine that compounds. That systems-thinking is what separates a real marketer from a 'social media person'. Save case study #2 in your portfolio folder.

Next week: social media marketing. You will take this content and learn the platform-specific tactics, algorithms, hashtags, engagement, and a 30-day growth plan, to actually grow Adwoa's following.

cards.prompt: A great piece of content can keep attracting customers for months, unlike an ad that stops when you stop paying.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Content is a durable, compounding asset. That is why building a content SYSTEM is so valuable for a small business.
cards.whenWrong: It is true. Content keeps working long after it is made; ads stop the instant you stop paying. Content compounds.

cards.prompt: Presenting your pillars + calendar + pieces as a 'system' shows employers you build systems, not just posts.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Systems-thinking is what separates a real marketer from a 'social media person'. Frame the work that way.
cards.whenWrong: It does. Showing a repeatable system (not random posts) is exactly the higher-value signal employers want.

cards.prompt: Case study #2 is throwaway practice, not something feeding the rest of the track.
cards.whenRight: Correct, the content and calendar directly feed Week 3's social plan and the awareness stage of your funnel. It is live material.
cards.whenWrong: It feeds forward, the ten pieces and calendar power next week's social growth plan. Real, reusable work.

items.body:

Two case studies done. Next week: social media marketing, turning this content into real follower and lead growth.

weeks.title: Social Media Marketing
weeks.context:
You have content. This week you learn to make it grow an actual audience. Social media marketing is the craft of using platforms (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, WhatsApp) to reach, engage, and convert your customer, working WITH each platform's algorithm instead of against it. The same content can reach 50 people or 50,000 depending on whether you understand how these platforms decide who sees what.

For Adwoa's Kitchen, social is where the awareness and consideration stages happen at scale. Food is built for social, it is visual, emotional, and shareable, so Adwoa has a real advantage if she plays it right. This week you learn the algorithm basics, which platforms matter for her, how hashtags and engagement actually work, and how to turn followers into leads (people who order or join the email list).

By Sunday you will have a complete 30-day social media growth plan: which platforms, what to post when, how to engage daily, hashtag strategy, and the specific tactics to move from zero toward the 10K goal. That plan is case study #3, and it is what you would actually execute to grow the account.

concept_check.q: Why does the Instagram or TikTok algorithm show some posts to thousands of people and others to almost no one?
choices: It is random
It tests each post on a small group; if they engage (watch, like, save, share, comment), it shows it to more people
It only shows posts from accounts that pay
It favours accounts with the most followers only
concept_check.explain: Algorithms test content on a small audience first. Strong early engagement (especially watch time, saves, and shares) signals 'this is good', so the platform shows it to more people. Weak engagement caps the reach.

concept_check.q: Adwoa has 100 followers and posts a beautiful photo, but it gets almost no reach. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Buy followers
Post more often and engage, plus use formats the algorithm pushes (like reels) and a strong hook
Delete the account and start over
Only post on weekends
concept_check.explain: Small accounts grow through reach-friendly formats (reels/short video), strong hooks, consistency, and active engagement. Buying followers is fake growth that hurts the algorithm and never converts.

concept_check.q: What is the difference between a follower and a lead?
choices: Nothing, they are the same
A follower watches your content; a lead has taken a step toward buying (ordered, joined your list, or messaged to enquire)
A lead is someone who unfollowed
A follower is more valuable than a lead
concept_check.explain: Followers are reach; leads are intent. The goal is to convert followers into leads (orders, enquiries, email signups). Ten thousand followers with no leads do not pay the bills, the plan must turn attention into action.

days.title: How algorithms work, and set up the accounts
days.summary: Today you'll understand how social algorithms decide reach, then set up Adwoa's business accounts and free scheduling tools.

items.title: The algorithm is a taste-tester
items.body:
## What an algorithm actually does
An algorithm is just the platform's system for deciding *who sees what*. There are billions of posts; it cannot show everyone everything, so it predicts what each user will most want to see and shows them that. Understanding this one idea changes how you post.

## The test-and-scale model
When you post, the platform shows it to a *small* sample of your audience first, a taste-test. It watches how they react: do they watch to the end? Like? Save? Share? Comment? If that small group engages strongly, the platform thinks 'this is good content' and shows it to a bigger group, then a bigger one. If they scroll past, reach stops. This is why two posts from the same account can reach 50 or 50,000 people, the difference is *early engagement*.

## What the algorithm rewards (in rough order of power)
1. **Watch time / completion** (for video), did they watch the whole reel?
2. **Shares and saves**, the strongest 'this is valuable' signals.
3. **Comments**, especially genuine conversation.
4. **Likes**, weakest but still counts.

Notice: a strong *hook* (Week 2) drives watch time, value content drives saves, and a question drives comments. Your content choices directly feed the signals the algorithm rewards. You are not gaming it, you are giving it what it (and your audience) wants.

## What hurts you
Buying followers (fake accounts do not engage, which *lowers* your average engagement and tanks reach), posting and disappearing, and content with no hook. Real growth comes from real engagement. There are no shortcuts that last.

This week you build a plan that works *with* this system: reach-friendly formats, strong hooks, consistency, and active engagement.

items.title: Set up business accounts and free tools
items.body:
## Get the accounts right
**1. Business accounts.** Convert Adwoa's Instagram and Facebook to *Business/Professional* accounts (free, in settings). This unlocks **Insights** (analytics: reach, engagement, follower data) and the ability to add a contact button and run ads later. A personal account hides all of this. On TikTok, switch to a Business account too. Without analytics you are flying blind.

**2. Meta Business Suite.** Go to business.facebook.com and connect Adwoa's Facebook + Instagram. Meta Business Suite (free) lets you *schedule* posts in advance, see insights across both, and manage messages in one place. Scheduling is what makes a calendar sustainable, plan a week, schedule it, done.

**3. A clear bio.** Each profile bio must do three jobs in one glance: say *what* (Homemade jollof, grills + spice mix, Accra), *who for* (a hint of the customer), and *what to do next* (the link / 'Order on WhatsApp'). The bio is prime real estate, it is where followers become leads.

**4. WhatsApp for orders.** Set up a WhatsApp number (ideally WhatsApp Business, free) as the ordering channel. In Ghana, WhatsApp is where many small-business sales actually close. Add the 'Message' button to the profiles.

Today is setup. The rest of the week is strategy and the 30-day plan.

cards.prompt: The algorithm shows your post to everyone at once and then stops.
cards.whenRight: Right, it tests on a small group first, then scales reach based on their engagement. Strong early engagement = more reach.
cards.whenWrong: It test-and-scales: a small sample first, then wider only if they engage. Early engagement decides total reach.

cards.prompt: Saves and shares are stronger 'this is valuable' signals than likes.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Saves and shares carry the most weight, then comments, then likes. Make content worth saving and sharing.
cards.whenWrong: They are. Saves and shares are the top signals (someone valued it enough to keep or pass on). Likes are the weakest.

cards.prompt: Buying followers is a smart shortcut to trigger the algorithm.
cards.whenRight: Right, it backfires. Fake followers do not engage, which lowers your engagement rate and reduces reach. It is fake, harmful growth.
cards.whenWrong: It hurts you. Bought followers never engage, dragging down your engagement rate and your reach. Avoid it entirely.

items.body:
Get Adwoa social-ready:

- [ ] Instagram (and Facebook/TikTok) switched to Business accounts
- [ ] Meta Business Suite connected for scheduling and insights
- [ ] Each bio rewritten to say what, who for, and what to do next
- [ ] WhatsApp set up as the ordering channel, with a Message button on profiles

Then write one sentence: based on the algorithm, which content format should Adwoa lean into most? (Hint: what drives watch time and shares for food?)

days.title: Orient, pick the right platforms
days.summary: Today you'll decide which platforms Adwoa should focus on, because winning one beats being mediocre on five.

items.title: Win one platform before adding another
items.body:
## Do not spread thin
The biggest social mistake small businesses make is trying to be everywhere, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, Pinterest, all at once, and doing all of them badly. Each platform takes real effort to win. Pick ONE primary platform to dominate and maybe one secondary, and ignore the rest until those are working. Depth beats breadth.

## How to choose (match platform to customer and content)
Two questions decide it: *Where is Akosua?* and *What content does this platform reward?*

- **Instagram** (Reels + feed + Stories): huge in Ghana for food, visual, strong for both reach (reels) and trust (stories/feed). Akosua scrolls it on her commute. **Strong primary candidate for Adwoa.**
- **TikTok**: fastest organic reach right now, short video, great for going viral with food content; younger-skewing but growing fast in Ghana. **Strong for reach (awareness).**
- **Facebook**: still massive in Ghana, especially for community groups, local selling, and an older audience; great for Marketplace and local reach. **Useful secondary, especially for local orders.**
- **WhatsApp**: not for discovery, but where sales *close* and where you can run a 'broadcast'/status to existing contacts. **The conversion layer, not the growth layer.**

## A sensible stack for Adwoa
Primary: **Instagram** (reels for reach, stories/feed for trust). Secondary: **TikTok** (reach via short video, repurpose the same reels). Conversion: **WhatsApp** (where orders close). Facebook as a light third for local groups. This focuses effort where the customer is and the content fits, and lets you repurpose one reel across IG and TikTok for double the reach with the same work.

Today you choose Adwoa's platforms and justify each. A clear choice now saves wasted effort all month.

cards.prompt: A small business should be active on as many platforms as possible from day one.
cards.whenRight: Right, win one (maybe two) first. Spreading across five means doing all badly. Depth beats breadth.
cards.whenWrong: No, focus. Dominate one primary platform, add a secondary, ignore the rest until those work.

cards.prompt: You should pick platforms based on where your customer is and what content the platform rewards.
cards.whenRight: Yes. Match platform to the persona's habits and to your content type. For visual food, Instagram and TikTok fit naturally.
cards.whenWrong: Those are the two right questions: where is your customer, and what content wins there. Match both.

cards.prompt: WhatsApp is mainly a discovery platform for finding new customers.
cards.whenRight: Right, it is a CONVERSION layer where orders close, not a discovery engine. Use IG/TikTok to find people, WhatsApp to sell.
cards.whenWrong: It is for closing, not discovery. New customers come from IG/TikTok; WhatsApp is where they place the order.

items.title: Your turn, choose the platforms
items.body:
Start your 30-day plan doc with the platform strategy:

- [ ] Choose a PRIMARY platform and write why (customer + content fit)
- [ ] Choose a SECONDARY platform and how you will repurpose content to it
- [ ] Name the CONVERSION channel (where orders close)
